## Medical vs. Research Accelerators — What Changes for AI

| | Research machine | Clinical medical machine |
|---|---|---|
| **Duty cycle** | Weeks of continuous runs | Daily sessions, maintenance gaps |
| **Downtime tolerance** | Hours–days acceptable | Patient appointments cannot be cancelled |
| **Fault event rate** | Can be high (discovery machine) | Designed to be *rare* — but that means scarce fault data |
| **Real-time budget** | Seconds to minutes per correction | ms to μs for pulse-to-pulse corrections |
| **Data volume** | Abundant if running continuously | Sparse — gaps between sessions |
| **Regulatory overhead** | Internal safety rules | IEC 62304, ISO 13485, FDA/CE mark for software |
| **Personnel** | Accelerator physicists | Clinical physicists + radiation therapists |

::: {.warning-box}
**The key inversion:** clinical machines are engineered to *avoid* faults — so fault data is scarce by design.
This is the opposite of the "big data" assumption most ML workflows make.
:::

::: notes
This table is the most important slide in the lecture. Everything else flows from it.

The "scarce fault data" row is the one that shapes the most design choices. On a research machine like SPIRAL2 you might have hundreds of quench events per run. On a clinical proton therapy machine, you might have one in six months — and it will have triggered an interlock before any data was captured.

This drives: transfer learning, data augmentation, physics-informed models, unsupervised anomaly detection (train only on normal data).

The regulatory row is worth a sentence: IEC 62304 is the software lifecycle standard for medical device software. Any AI running in a clinical control loop is in scope. This requires audit trails, change management, and explainability — not as extras, but as compliance requirements.
:::

# Use Case 1 {.section-divider background-color="#0a1520"}

::: {style="color: #22d3ee; font-size: 1.6em; font-weight: 800; margin-top: 0.5em;"}
RF Fault Detection
:::

Autoencoders on cavity waveforms

---

## The RF Fault Detection Problem

::: {.col-left}
**Every RF pulse generates a waveform.**

On a superconducting cavity:

- Forward power, reflected power
- Cavity field amplitude and phase → **IQ signals** (in-phase + quadrature)
- One pair of waveforms per cavity per pulse (~1 kHz repetition rate)

**A fault shows up in the waveform** — but often subtly:

- Quench: sudden amplitude drop
- Trip: instant zero crossing
- Detuning: Q component becomes nonzero (cavity goes off-resonance)
- Multipacting: oscillations during flat-top

:::

::: {.col-right}
::: {.highlight-box}
**Why this is hard:**

Clinical machines are designed to be safe → faults are rare → you have very few labelled fault examples.

**Supervised classifier:** needs thousands of examples of each fault class.

**Autoencoder:** trained on *normal* pulses only. Faults have high reconstruction error. No fault labels needed.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.key-result}
Train on normal. Flag the unusual.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: notes
IQ signals: the RF signal at cavity resonance frequency is demodulated into in-phase (I) and quadrature (Q) components. On a well-tuned on-resonance cavity, I is a trapezoidal pulse (fill → flat-top → decay) and Q is near zero. Any off-resonance operation or fault appears in the Q signal.

The autoencoder approach is well-suited here: you need only normal data for training, and you define "anomaly" as "the model can't reconstruct this." This is deployed in production at JLab (CEBAF), SNS at Oak Ridge, and in our research at GANIL/SPIRAL2.
:::

---

## Synthetic RF Waveforms — What the Data Looks Like

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-align: center

# This cell runs at render time to produce the figure
# (see notebooks/01_fault_detection/generate_data.py for the full generator)
import numpy as np
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

def _envelope(t, rise=0.10, fall=0.85):
    return np.piecewise(t.astype(float),
        [t < rise, (t >= rise) & (t <= fall), t > fall],
        [lambda t: t / rise, 1.0, lambda t: (1.0 - t) / (1.0 - fall)])

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
t = np.linspace(0, 1, 256)
noise = 0.025

def normal(seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    env = _envelope(t)
    return env + rng.normal(0, noise, 256), rng.normal(0, noise, 256)

def quench(seed=1):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    I, Q = normal(seed)
    qp = rng.integers(80, 160)
    I[qp:] = rng.normal(0, noise/2, 256-qp)
    Q[qp:] = rng.normal(0, noise/2, 256-qp)
    return I, Q

def detuning(seed=2):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    env = _envelope(t)
    freq = rng.uniform(3, 7)
    I = env * np.cos(2*np.pi*freq*t) + rng.normal(0, noise, 256)
    Q = env * np.sin(2*np.pi*freq*t) + rng.normal(0, noise, 256)
    return I, Q

def multipacting(seed=3):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    I, Q = normal(seed)
    s, e = 40, 210
    freq = rng.uniform(6, 12)
    amp = rng.uniform(0.12, 0.22)
    tt = np.linspace(0, 1, e-s)
    I[s:e] += amp * np.sin(2*np.pi*freq*tt)
    Q[s:e] += amp * np.cos(2*np.pi*freq*tt)
    return I, Q

cases = [("Normal", normal, "#22d3ee"), ("Quench", quench, "#f87171"),
         ("Detuning", detuning, "#fb923c"), ("Multipacting", multipacting, "#a78bfa")]

fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=4,
    subplot_titles=[f"{n} — I" for n,_,_ in cases] + [f"{n} — Q" for n,_,_ in cases],
    vertical_spacing=0.12, horizontal_spacing=0.06)

for col, (name, fn, color) in enumerate(cases, 1):
    I, Q = fn()
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=I, line=dict(color=color, width=1.5),
                             name=name, showlegend=(col==1)), row=1, col=col)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=t, y=Q, line=dict(color=color, width=1.5),
                             showlegend=False), row=2, col=col)

fig.update_layout(
    height=420, paper_bgcolor="#0d1b2a", plot_bgcolor="#111f30",
    font=dict(color="#e2e8f0", size=11),
    margin=dict(l=30, r=10, t=50, b=10),
    legend=dict(orientation="h", y=1.12, x=0.5, xanchor="center",
                font=dict(color="#e2e8f0")),
)
fig.update_xaxes(showgrid=False, zeroline=False, color="#475569")
fig.update_yaxes(showgrid=True, gridcolor="#1e3048", zeroline=False, color="#475569")
fig.show()
```

::: notes
This figure is generated by the synthetic data generator. Each column is a fault class. Row 1 is the I (in-phase) component; row 2 is Q (quadrature).

Note: for a normal on-resonance pulse, Q is near zero. Detuning shows strong Q signal — this is the cavity going off-resonance. Quench shows a sudden drop in both I and Q at some point in the flat-top. Multipacting shows oscillations.

In the companion notebook, participants generate this dataset themselves and explore it interactively.
:::

## Autoencoder for Anomaly Detection — The Model

```{python}
import torch, torch.nn as nn

class RFAutoencoder(nn.Module):
    """1-D conv autoencoder for IQ waveform anomaly detection."""

    def __init__(self, seq_len=256, latent_dim=16):
        super().__init__()
        # Encoder: 2 channels (I + Q) → latent vector
        self.encoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv1d(2, 32, kernel_size=8, stride=4, padding=2),   # → 64
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.Conv1d(32, 64, kernel_size=4, stride=2, padding=1),  # → 32
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.Flatten(),
            nn.Linear(64 * 32, latent_dim),
        )
        # Decoder: latent → reconstructed waveform
        self.decoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(latent_dim, 64 * 32),
            nn.Unflatten(1, (64, 32)),
            nn.ConvTranspose1d(64, 32, kernel_size=4, stride=2, padding=1),
            nn.GELU(),
            nn.ConvTranspose1d(32, 2, kernel_size=8, stride=4, padding=2),
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.decoder(self.encoder(x))

# Anomaly score: mean squared reconstruction error per pulse
def score(model, x):
    with torch.no_grad():
        return ((x - model(x)) ** 2).mean(dim=(1, 2))  # → shape (batch,)
```

::: notes
Two things to highlight here:

1. The input is shape `(batch, 2, 256)` — 2 channels (I and Q), 256 time points. We process both channels simultaneously with a shared encoder.

2. We train this on normal pulses only. At inference, we compute the mean squared reconstruction error per pulse. Normal pulses → low error. Faults → high error (the model has never seen them and can't reconstruct them well).

This is the autoencoder anomaly detection paradigm, first applied to SRF cavities at JLab (Tennant et al., 2020).
:::

---

## Training + Result

```{python}
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset

# Training — only on NORMAL pulses (label == 0)
model = RFAutoencoder(seq_len=256, latent_dim=16)
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)

X_normal = X_train[y_train == 0]           # shape: (N, 2, 256)
loader   = DataLoader(TensorDataset(X_normal), batch_size=64, shuffle=True)

for epoch in range(40):
    for (batch,) in loader:
        loss = ((batch - model(batch)) ** 2).mean()
        optimizer.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); optimizer.step()

# Inference: score every pulse (normal + faults)
scores = score(model, X_test)              # shape: (N_test,)

# Threshold at 95th percentile of normal-pulse scores
threshold = scores[y_test == 0].quantile(0.95)
predictions = (scores > threshold).long()  # 0 = normal, 1 = anomaly
```

::: {.key-result}
Trained on ~800 normal pulses · Tested on 200 normal + 600 fault pulses
:::

**Notebook 01** — run this yourself
`github.com/aghribi/cas2026-ai-medical-accelerators`
`notebooks/01_fault_detection/notebook.ipynb`
:::

::: notes
Key points:
- Training set: only normal pulses. No fault labels required.
- The threshold is set empirically — typically at the 95th percentile of normal-pulse reconstruction errors, so the false-positive rate on normal data is ~5%.
- In a real deployment, you tune this threshold based on the cost of false positives (unnecessary beam stops) vs false negatives (missed faults).

Beam Tuning with Bayesian Optimisation

Cheetah · differentiable accelerator simulation

---

## The Daily Startup Problem

::: {.col-left}
**Every morning on a clinical machine:**

1. Run QA checks (output, flatness, energy)
2. Tune steering magnets and quadrupoles until beam quality is within spec
3. Hand off to clinical staff

Currently: **20–45 min of physicist time**, largely manual.

The physics: *n* corrector magnets × *k* quadrupoles → high-dimensional space.
Grid search is exponential. Manual tuning is expert-dependent.

::: {.fragment}
**What "good beam" means at the nozzle:**

- Spot size σ < spec (e.g. 5 mm at isocentre)
- Energy spread < 1%
- Beam position within ±1 mm
:::
:::

::: {.col-right}
::: {.highlight-box}
**Bayesian Optimisation is a natural fit:**

- Works in 2–20 dimensions (realistic number of tunable elements)
- Sample-efficient: finds a good solution in ~50 evaluations vs. thousands for grid search
- Each "evaluation" = one beam measurement = seconds, not hours
- Can incorporate prior knowledge (expected optimal region)
:::

::: {.key-result .fragment}
Demonstrated at AWAKE (CERN), FLASH (DESY), and several clinical proton therapy centres.
:::
:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: notes
The sample efficiency point is critical. On a clinical machine, every beam measurement takes time and uses up machine availability. You want an algorithm that finds a good solution in as few evaluations as possible — Bayesian optimisation is designed for exactly this.

The surrogate model inside BO (typically a Gaussian Process) is updated after each measurement and used to propose the next point. This is fundamentally different from gradient descent (which requires a differentiable objective) and from grid search (which requires exponentially many evaluations).
:::

---

## Cheetah — Differentiable Beam Physics Simulator

::: {.col-left}
**What Cheetah is:**

- PyTorch-based fast beam dynamics simulation
- Models drifts, quadrupoles, dipoles, RF cavities, solenoids
- Differentiable → gradients flow through the simulation
- Runs on CPU or GPU in milliseconds
- Open source: `pip install cheetah-accelerator`

**Why it matters here:**

- We use Cheetah *as the "machine"* in the notebook
- Tune a virtual linac section, see the beam respond
- Same code structure you'd use with a real machine via an interface layer
:::

::: {.col-right}

```{python}
import torch
import cheetah

# Build a simple medical linac section
# (e.g., a proton therapy transport line)
segment = cheetah.Segment(elements=[
    cheetah.Drift(length=torch.tensor(0.5)),
    cheetah.Quadrupole(length=torch.tensor(0.1), name="QF1"),
    cheetah.Drift(length=torch.tensor(1.0)),
    cheetah.Quadrupole(length=torch.tensor(0.1), name="QD1"),
    cheetah.Drift(length=torch.tensor(0.5)),
    cheetah.Screen(name="monitor"),
])

# 150 MeV proton beam (typical proton therapy energy)
# total energy = kinetic (150 MeV) + proton rest mass (938.3 MeV)
beam_in = cheetah.ParameterBeam.from_twiss(
    energy=torch.tensor(1088.3e6),   # total energy in eV
    beta_x=torch.tensor(1.0),        # Twiss beta in m
    beta_y=torch.tensor(1.0),
    emittance_x=torch.tensor(1e-6),  # geometric emittance m·rad
    emittance_y=torch.tensor(1e-6),
    species=cheetah.Species("proton"),
)
```

:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: notes
Cheetah was originally developed at DESY for the AWAKE experiment and the European XFEL. It has since been adopted widely, including for research on therapy linac tuning.

The key point: the code structure for tuning a Cheetah segment is identical to what you'd write for a real machine — you just replace `cheetah.segment(beam)` with a call to your machine's measurement interface. This is why Cheetah is pedagogically perfect: students learn the algorithm, not the machine-specific interface.
:::

---

## Bayesian Optimisation Loop

```{python}
from skopt import gp_minimize
from skopt.space import Real

# Objective function: pass k1 values → run Cheetah → return beam size
def objective(params):
    k1_qf, k1_qd = params

    segment.QF1.k1 = torch.tensor(k1_qf, dtype=torch.float32)
    segment.QD1.k1 = torch.tensor(k1_qd, dtype=torch.float32)

    beam_out = segment.track(beam_in)
    sigma_x  = beam_out.sigma_x.item()
    sigma_y  = beam_out.sigma_y.item()

    return sigma_x + sigma_y   # minimise total RMS beam size at monitor

# Search space: k1 in [-5, 5] T/m² for each quad
space = [Real(-5.0, 5.0, name="k1_QF1"),
         Real(-5.0, 5.0, name="k1_QD1")]

result = gp_minimize(
    func=objective,
    dimensions=space,
    n_calls=40,          # 40 beam measurements — compare to ~500 for grid
    n_initial_points=8,  # random exploration before GP kicks in
    random_state=42,
    verbose=False,
)

print(f"Optimal k1_QF = {result.x[0]:.3f} T/m²")
print(f"Optimal k1_QD = {result.x[1]:.3f} T/m²")
print(f"Minimum beam size: {result.fun*1e3:.2f} mm")
```

::: {.qr-box}
**Notebook 02** — `notebooks/02_beam_tuning/notebook.ipynb`
Run on Colab · compare BO vs random search · see convergence curve
:::

::: notes
`skopt.gp_minimize` wraps a Gaussian Process surrogate inside a standard Bayesian optimisation loop. It's one of the most accessible BO libraries for teaching.

In the notebook, participants also compare this to:
1. Random search (same number of evaluations, much worse result)
2. Gradient descent through Cheetah (works because Cheetah is differentiable — a bonus section showing the power of differentiable simulation)

The 40-call budget is realistic for a morning startup scenario on a real machine where each measurement takes ~30 seconds.
:::

:::

---

## The Speed Problem

::: {.col-left}
**Tracking codes are slow.**

| Code | Typical runtime per evaluation |
|---|---|
| TraceWin (RFQ/LINAC) | 1–10 min |
| G4beamline (Geant4) | 10–60 min |
| FLUKA (dosimetry) | Hours |
| Cheetah (surrogate!) | ~2 ms |

For real-time control or online optimisation, you need millisecond response — not minutes.

**The solution:** train a neural network on simulation outputs.
Call the NN instead of the simulator during optimisation.
:::

::: {.col-right}
::: {.highlight-box}
**What a surrogate replaces:**

```
[Accelerator parameters]
        ↓  (seconds to hours)
  Tracking code
        ↓
  [Beam properties at output]
```

becomes:

```
[Accelerator parameters]
        ↓  (< 1 ms)
  Neural network surrogate
        ↓
  [Predicted beam properties]
```
:::

::: {.key-result .fragment}
Speedup of 10³–10⁵× · with <2% error in typical regimes
:::
:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: notes
This is the most widely deployed AI technique in accelerator physics today. Surrogate models (also called emulators or metamodels) are used at CERN for FCC design studies, at JLab for CEBAF operations, and in proton therapy for dose calculation acceleration (though the latter is on the treatment planning side).

On the accelerator side, surrogates are used for:
1. Real-time beam quality prediction (replace Cheetah or TraceWin in an online control loop)
2. Optimisation (run BO or RL against the surrogate instead of the real simulator)
3. Virtual commissioning of machines that don't exist yet (IFMIF-DONES example)
:::

---

## Building the Surrogate — Generate + Train

```{python}
import numpy as np, torch, torch.nn as nn
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, TensorDataset

# ── Step 1: Generate training data with Cheetah ───────────────────────────────
N = 5_000
k1_samples = torch.FloatTensor(N, 2).uniform_(-5.0, 5.0)   # random quad settings

beam_props = []
for k1_qf, k1_qd in k1_samples:
    segment.QF1.k1 = k1_qf
    segment.QD1.k1 = k1_qd
    b = segment.track(beam_in)
    beam_props.append([b.sigma_x.item(), b.sigma_y.item(),
                       b.mu_x.item(),    b.mu_y.item()])

y_data = torch.tensor(beam_props, dtype=torch.float32)   # shape (5000, 4)

# ── Step 2: Train a simple MLP surrogate ─────────────────────────────────────
surrogate = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(2, 128), nn.Tanh(),
    nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.Tanh(),
    nn.Linear(128, 4),             # predict σ_x, σ_y, μ_x, μ_y
)

optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(surrogate.parameters(), lr=3e-3)
loader = DataLoader(TensorDataset(k1_samples, y_data), batch_size=128, shuffle=True)

for epoch in range(200):
    for X_b, y_b in loader:
        pred = surrogate(X_b)
        loss = nn.functional.mse_loss(pred, y_b)
        optimizer.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); optimizer.step()
```

::: notes
Two design choices worth explaining:

1. **Tanh activation**: for a surrogate of smooth physics, Tanh often outperforms ReLU because it produces smoother interpolations between training points.

2. **Training data generation**: we use Latin Hypercube Sampling (or uniform random here for simplicity) to efficiently cover the parameter space. In production, you'd use an adaptive sampling strategy that concentrates points in regions of high curvature.

In the notebook, participants also see: (a) the accuracy metrics (R², MAE), (b) a predicted-vs-actual scatter plot, and (c) the timing comparison.
:::

---

## Surrogate vs. Cheetah — Speed and Accuracy

```{python}
import time

# Timing: Cheetah vs surrogate for 1000 evaluations
test_params = torch.FloatTensor(1000, 2).uniform_(-5.0, 5.0)

t0 = time.perf_counter()
for k1_qf, k1_qd in test_params:                  # Cheetah: one call at a time
    segment.QF1.k1 = k1_qf
    segment.QD1.k1 = k1_qd
    _ = segment.track(beam_in)
t_cheetah = time.perf_counter() - t0              # typically ~2 s for 1000 calls

t0 = time.perf_counter()
with torch.no_grad():
    _ = surrogate(test_params)                     # surrogate: batched, < 5 ms
t_surrogate = time.perf_counter() - t0

print(f"Cheetah  : {t_cheetah*1e3:.0f} ms for 1000 evals")
print(f"Surrogate: {t_surrogate*1e3:.1f} ms for 1000 evals")
print(f"Speedup  : {t_cheetah/t_surrogate:.0f}×")

# Accuracy
with torch.no_grad():
    y_pred = surrogate(test_params)
y_true = torch.tensor([...])   # pre-computed Cheetah outputs for test_params
mae = (y_pred - y_true).abs().mean(dim=0)
print(f"MAE σ_x: {mae[0]*1e3:.2f} mm  |  MAE σ_y: {mae[1]*1e3:.2f} mm")
```

::: notes
Typical results on the synthetic dataset:
- Cheetah: ~2 ms per evaluation → 2 s for 1000 calls
- Surrogate: ~4 ms for 1000 batched calls → **~500× speedup**

The accuracy is typically sub-percent for σ_x and σ_y in the interpolation regime (within the training data range). Extrapolation degrades gracefully.

The notebook bonus section uses the surrogate inside the Bayesian optimisation from notebook 02, so participants can compare:
- BO with Cheetah as oracle: 40 × 2 ms = 80 ms
- BO with a physical machine: 40 × 30 s = 20 min
- BO with a TraceWin surrogate: 40 × 5 min → now 40 × 0.001 ms

This is the case where the surrogate becomes transformative: replacing a 3-hour computation with a 5-minute one.
:::

## From Surrogate to Digital Twin

::: {.col-left}

A surrogate answers: *"What does the simulation predict?"*

A **digital twin** answers: *"What is my actual machine doing right now?"*

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│         Digital Twin                │
│                                     │
│  Physics sim  ─┐                    │
│  (offline)     │→  ML surrogate  ─┐ │
│                │   (fast, diff.)  │ │
│  Live sensors ─┘                  │→│→ Real-time state estimate
│  (BPMs, BLMs, RF diagnostics)    │ │   + control recommendation
│                                   │ │
│  Anomaly detector ────────────────┘ │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘
```

:::

::: {.col-right}
**Medical accelerator use cases:**

- **Virtual commissioning** — test control strategies before beam-on
- **Adaptive QA** — twin detects drift, flags recalibration
- **Fault simulation** — inject virtual faults to train operators
- **Cross-facility learning** — twin trained at one centre, adapted to another

::: {.key-result .fragment}
TwinRISE (Horizon Europe, 2026–2030): building trusted, federated digital twins for research and medical accelerators across 19 institutions in 7 countries.
:::
:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: notes
The distinction between surrogate and digital twin is important. A surrogate is a fast model of the simulation. A digital twin adds the live data layer: it continuously ingests sensor readings and maintains a real-time state estimate of the actual machine, diverging from the physics simulation when reality deviates.

TwinRISE is the Horizon project I'm coordinating at GANIL. One of the seven use cases is exactly this: a federated digital twin that learns from SPIRAL2 (superconducting LINAC) and KARA (storage ring) and transfers to new machines.

The "cross-facility learning" point is the federated learning angle: you train model updates locally at each site and share only gradients, preserving data sovereignty.
:::

---

## Open Problems — What AI Cannot Yet Solve Here

::: {.col-left}

**1. Data scarcity on clinical machines**

- Fault data is rare by design
- Transfer learning from research machines is promising but not solved
- Few-shot and physics-informed approaches are active research areas

**2. Explainability for regulatory compliance**

- IEC 62304 requires interpretable decisions in the control loop
- SHAP values, attention maps, prototype explanations are partial solutions
- "Why did the model flag this pulse?" must have an auditable answer

**3. Cross-facility transfer**

- A model trained at Centre A rarely works at Centre B without retraining
- Federated learning + domain adaptation are the frontier
:::

::: {.col-right}

**4. Control system integration**

- Clinical LINACs run proprietary interfaces (Varian, Elekta, IBA)
- Deploying a Python model inside a real-time control system is an engineering challenge as much as a scientific one
- OPC-UA, EPICS adapters are the pragmatic path

**5. Foundation models for accelerators**

- No pre-trained accelerator model exists yet (analogous to LLMs)
- Would require pooled data across facilities — a governance challenge
- ARTIFACT / TwinRISE are building the infrastructure for this

::: {.key-result style="margin-top: 1em;"}
These are research problems — not blockers.
AI is already deployed and delivering value in clinical accelerator operations today.
:::
:::

::: {.clearfix}
:::

::: notes
I want to be honest about what isn't solved. This is a school lecture, not a marketing presentation.

The data scarcity problem is the most fundamental. It shapes every design choice: why we use autoencoders (unsupervised), why we use Bayesian optimisation (sample-efficient), why we use physics-informed neural networks (can work with very little data by leveraging known equations).

On explainability: the EU AI Act (2024) classifies AI in safety-critical control systems as "high-risk." This means conformity assessment, human oversight, and documentation. For a fault classifier, that means: not just "this is a fault" but "this is a fault *because* the Q signal shows a characteristic pattern consistent with detuning."

The foundation model question is the 5-year horizon. If we could pool cavity waveform data from all superconducting accelerators in Europe — which is the goal of the ARTIFACT FAIR data store — we could pre-train a model that any facility could fine-tune on their local data. That's the vision. We're building the infrastructure now.
:::

---

## Summary — Three Things to Take Away

::: {.col-left}

::: {.key-result}
**1. Medical accelerators invert the ML problem**

Clinical constraints (safety, uptime, regulation) mean less data and stricter requirements.
Design for scarcity: autoencoders, Bayesian optimisation, physics-informed models.
:::

::: {.key-result style="margin-top: 0.6em;"}
**2. Three AI categories, all deployable today**

- Fault detection (autoencoders on RF waveforms)
- Beam tuning (Bayesian optimisation, RL)
- Surrogate models (neural networks as fast simulators)
:::
